dc.description.abstract.value:
Summary of the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963
Key Provisions
1.	Constitution of Boards
•	Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)
•	Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) (previously Central Board of Excise and Customs, amended in 2018)
•	Membership: Up to 7 members appointed by the Central Government for each Board.
2.	Tax Domains
•	Direct Taxes (CBDT): Includes Income-tax, Wealth-tax, Estate Duty, Gift-tax, and other taxes as specified or declared by the Central Government.
•	Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC): Implies oversight of excise, customs, and other indirect taxes, though detailed definitions are not provided in the excerpt.
3.	Operational Framework
•	Powers and Duties: Exercised under the control of the Central Government, with duties entrusted by law or by the Government.
•	Rule Making: The Central Government may make rules to regulate the transaction of business by each Board.
4.	Legislative Amendments
•	Enactment Updates: Modifications to various Acts (e.g., Estate Duty Act, 1953; Customs Act, 1962) to align with the new Board structures.
•	Transfer of Functions: Responsibilities of the old Central Board of Revenue are divided based on tax type.
5.	Procedural and Transitional Provisions
•	Transfer of Pending Proceedings: Cases before the old Board are transferred to the appropriate new Board, with disputes resolved by the Central Government.
•	Difficulty Resolution: The Central Government can issue orders to address implementation challenges.
•	Repeal and Saving Clause: Repeals the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1924, while safeguarding previous actions.

dc.description.abstract.value:
summary of the Remittances of Foreign Exchange and Investment in Foreign Exchange Bonds (Immunities and Exemptions) Act, 1991:
Objective:
To attract large inflows of foreign exchange by providing immunities and exemptions to persons receiving remittances in foreign exchange and owning Foreign Exchange Bonds.
Key Components:
1.	Remittances of Foreign Exchange
•	Definitions:
•	Recipient: Person in India receiving remittances.
•	Remittance: Foreign exchange received in specified forms from outside India, between the Act's commencement and a specified date (initially 1st December 1991).
•	Immunities (Section 3):
•	No disclosure required on the nature and source of remittance.
•	No inquiry/investigation can be initiated based on receiving such remittances.
•	Remittance details are inadmissible as evidence in certain proceedings.
•	Exemptions (Section 4):
•	Remittances not considered for income tax purposes (though income from remittances is taxable).
•	Not included in net wealth for wealth tax purposes for assessments before 1st April 1992.
2.	Investment in Foreign Exchange Bonds
•	Definitions:
•	Foreign Exchange Bonds: Issued by the State Bank of India under a specified scheme, for investments made between the Act's commencement and a specified date (initially 1st December 1991).
•	Non-Resident Indian (NRI) and Overseas Corporate Body definitions provided.
•	Immunities (Section 6):
•	Similar to those for remittances: no disclosure, no inquiries based on bond ownership, and inadmissibility of bond ownership as evidence.
•	Exceptions for foreign exchange not brought into India as required by other laws.
•	Exemptions (Section 7):
•	Interest from bonds not subject to income tax.
•	Bonds not subject to wealth tax.
•	Gifts of bonds not subject to gift tax under certain conditions.
Scope and Exceptions:
•	Extent: Whole of India.
•	Exceptions to Immunities:
•	For foreign exchange required to be brought into India under other laws with unexpired periods.
•	For prosecutions under specific criminal laws (e.g., Indian Penal Code, Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act) and civil liability enforcement.
Administration:
•	Schemes for remittances and bond investments to be laid before Parliament by the Central Government.

indexableObject.name: Procedure in sale of immovable property.

dc.identifier.section_page_note.value:
In the sale of immovable property under this Act the following rules shall be observed:—
First.- The sale shall be by public auction to the highest bidder. The time and place of sale shall be fixed by the Collector of the district in which the property is situated, or other officer empowered by the Collector in that behalf. The time may be either previous to or after the expiration of the fasli year.
Second.—Previous to the sale the Collector, or other officer empowered by the Collector in that behalf, shall issue a notice thereof in English and in the language of the district, specifying the name of the defaulter; the position and extent of land and of his buildings thereon; the amount of revenue assessed on the land, or upon its different sections; the proportion of the public revenue due during the remainder of the current fasli; and the time, place, and conditions of sale. This notice shall be fixed up one month at least before the sale in the Collector's office and in the Taluk cutcherry, in the nearest police station-house, and on some conspicuous part of the land.
Third.—A sum of money equal to fifteen per cent of the price of the land shall be deposited by the purchaser in the hands of the Collector, or other officer empowered by the Collector in that behalf, at the time of the purchase, and where the remainder of the purchase-money may not be paid within thirty days, the money so deposited shall be liable to forfeiture.
Fourth.—Where the purchaser may refuse or omit to deposit the said sum of money, or to complete the payment of the remaining purchase-money, the property shall be resold at the expense and hazard of such purchaser, and the amount of all loss or expense which may attend such refusal or omission shall be recoverable from such purchaser in the same manner as arrears of public revenue. Where the lands may, on the second sale, sell for a higher price than at the first sale, the difference or increase shall be the property of him on whose account the said first sale was made.
Fifth.- All persons bidding at a sale may be required to state whether they are bidding on their own behalf or as agents, and, in the latter case, to deposit a written authority signed by their principals. If such requisition be not complied with, their bids may be rejected.
